PROJECT KAAMADHENU
The Sacred Cow Shelter of Srimad Sai Rajarajeshwari Ashram
A Story of Compassion, Devotion, and Sustainable Living
The cow is our mother. She nourishes us as we grow. Protecting her is not tradition — it is gratitude.
Amma's Vision: The Divine Mother Who Walks the Path

At the heart of Project Kaamadhenu is a Divine person — a spiritual teacher whose life is itself a teaching. Srimad Sai Rajarajeshwari, lovingly called Amma by her devotees, is the founder and guiding light of the Ashram. Her connection to the care of cows is not incidental. It is central to her spiritual path and to the mission of the entire institution she has built.
A Life Rooted in Devotion

As described in Ashram literature, Amma was born on 29 March 1947 in Mangalore, Karnataka, India, into a deeply spiritual family that had prayed fervently for the Divine Mother to be born among them. Her earliest years were shaped by the presence of saints and sages, and by a household atmosphere of prayer, selflessness, and devotion. The revered saint Ramdas of Kanhangad, recognizing her divine radiance, named her Lalitha — a sacred epithet of the Divine Mother, Lalitha Tripura Sundari.

Ancient Nadi readings — palm-leaf manuscripts inscribed by sages thousands of years ago — describe Amma in extraordinary terms. The Agastya Nadi places her in the same spiritual stature as the beloved saint Shirdi Sai Baba. The Budha Nadi records her as Omkara, Sreemkara, Hreemkara Roopini — embodying the three primordial cosmic sounds — and as Vasudeva Maya Durga, a form of the supreme divine feminine.

For devotees, Amma is not merely a teacher of spiritual truths. She is a living embodiment of the divine — and her choices about how to live, what to build, and where to direct the Ashram's energies carry profound meaning.
Walking the Path: Leading by Example

In Hindu spiritual tradition, there is a principle called Acharana — embodied living, or walking the path rather than merely speaking about it. A true spiritual teacher does not only deliver discourses and write scriptures. They live the teaching in every act of daily life.

Amma's establishment and deep personal commitment to the Goshala is exactly this kind of embodied leadership. In a world where the plight of cows — their exploitation in industrial dairy systems, their slaughter at the end of their productive lives, the separation of calves from mothers — is increasingly a matter of global ethical concern, Amma has chosen to respond not with words alone but with action. She has built a sanctuary. She has created systems that honour the full life of every animal in her care. She has modelled, on a meaningful scale, what it looks like to truly treat the cow as a sacred mother rather than as a resource to be extracted from and discarded.

The Journey of Project Kaamadhenu: Twenty Years of Growth
Every great institution begins with a single step. Project Kaamadhenu began with two cows.
The Beginning: Two Cows and a Sacred Intention

Approximately twenty years ago, the Goshala was established at the Ashram with just two cows. It was a modest beginning by any measure — two animals, a small shelter, a handful of devoted caregivers, and an enormous amount of love. But it was animated from the very first day by a clarity of vision and a depth of spiritual commitment that would allow it to grow far beyond what anyone might have initially imagined.

Those first two cows were not merely animals kept for their milk. They were the beginning of a covenant — a promise that here, at this Ashram, the ancient relationship between human beings and cows would be honoured in its fullness. That no animal would be discarded when their usefulness diminished. That bulls would not be sold to slaughter. That every cow, every calf, every bull would live out their natural lives in safety, dignity, and love.

It is worth pausing on that commitment, because it is not a small thing. In the prevailing economy of cattle in India today — as in most parts of the world — bulls are economically inconvenient. They do not produce milk. They require significant food and care. The market logic is to sell them, and in the absence of buyers for agricultural labour (itself increasingly mechanised), they are frequently sent to slaughterhouses. It takes a genuine counter-cultural commitment, backed by substantial financial resources and organisational will, to say: not here. Here, every life is honoured.
Twenty Years of Growth: From Two to Three Hundred +

From those two founding cows, the Goshala has grown steadily over two decades into one of the most significant cow sanctuaries in the region. Today, Project Kaamadhenu is home to more than 300 animals — a vibrant, bustling, beloved community of cows, bulls, and approximately 80 calves.

This growth did not happen by accident. It happened because of sustained commitment — financial, organisational, and spiritual. It happened because of the generosity of devotees and donors who understood that protecting cows is not just a matter of religious sentiment but of genuine compassion. It happened because of the tireless, unglamorous, daily work of the Ashram staff and volunteers who care for these animals every single day of the year, in every kind of weather, through illness and through celebration.

It happened, most fundamentally, because Amma built an institution with the structures needed to sustain it — not just the infrastructure of shelters and feeding systems and waste management, but the infrastructure of purpose: a community of people who understand why this work matters and who are committed to continuing it for generations to come.
